subject: Agriculture
title: Satellite Crop Monitoring
description: Learn Satellite Crop Monitoring in one minute.

hook.text: Satellites photograph every field on Earth every five days. Governments use this data to predict harvests before they happen.

buildup.text: NASA's Landsat and ESA's Sentinel satellites provide free imagery that tracks crop growth at 10-meter resolution.

discovery.text: USDA uses satellite data to forecast global crop production—moving commodity markets billions of dollars on report day.

twist.text: Hedge funds buy commercial satellite data to predict harvests before official reports—gaining trading advantages.

climax.text: Developing countries use satellite monitoring for food security early warning—detecting droughts before famine unfolds.

punchline.text: Satellites see your crops from space. Who sees them first decides who profits.

quiz.question: How often do modern satellites photograph every field on Earth?

details.summary: Satellite crop monitoring uses orbital sensors to track vegetation health, soil moisture, and growth patterns across vast areas. This topic explains NDVI indices, remote sensing platforms, and how satellite data helps farmers make timely management decisions.
details.whyItMatters: Satellites can monitor millions of hectares simultaneously, giving governments and farmers early warnings about droughts, pest outbreaks, and yield forecasts at a fraction of ground-survey costs.
takeaways: NDVI imagery reveals crop health by measuring reflected near-infrared light
Free satellite data from Sentinel and Landsat is accessible to any farmer
Satellite monitoring enables early drought detection and yield forecasting

faq.question: How does satellite crop monitoring work?
faq.answer: Satellites capture images in visible and near-infrared wavelengths. Vegetation indices like NDVI measure how much light plants absorb versus reflect, revealing crop vigor, stress, and growth stage across entire fields or regions.

faq.question: Is satellite crop monitoring available to small farmers?
faq.answer: Yes. Programs like ESA's Sentinel and NASA's Landsat provide free imagery. Many agtech platforms process this data into simple maps and alerts that smallholder farmers can access via smartphone apps.
